papers.title: Impact of Testosterone on Daily Wheel Running in Female Rats.
papers.abstract: Sex differences in daily activity have been attributed to the actions of gonadal steroid hormones. We tested this hypothesis by measuring the impact of male-typical levels of testosterone (T) on female rats' daily activity. Analyses were conducted on pooled data from three studies in which adult female Sprague-Dawley rats were implanted with blank or T-filled capsules (and adult males were implanted with blank capsules); home cage wheel running activity was measured 23 h/day before and for 3 weeks after capsule implantation. Approximately 75-80% of running occurred during the dark phase of the light-dark cycle in all groups, throughout the study. Before capsule implantation, the total number of wheel revolutions was significantly higher in females than males at the end of the light phase and during most of the dark phase; running speed and duration of daily running were higher in females compared to males. During the 3 weeks after capsule implantation, dark phase (and end-of-light phase) wheel revolutions, and average and maximum running speeds increased in all groups; however, T exposure blunted females' running increases during the second half of the dark phase, such that running during that period was similar to that of males by week 3. T also decreased the duration of females' active time, primarily by shifting offset of wheel running earlier, making it comparable to that in males. T non-significantly decreased females' running speeds. These results indicate that, within 3 weeks, T defeminizes females' daily activity in multiple ways. Thus, in addition to producing myriad physiological changes, male-typical levels of T also alter females' locomotor behavior.

papers.title: Microgravity and Cardiac Electrophysiology: Autonomic Remodeling, Arrhythmogenesis, and Implications for Long-Duration Spaceflight.
papers.abstract: In microgravity, the human heart undergoes significant geometric and functional remodeling due to the removal of gravity-dependent hydrostatic gradients. These adaptations include a transition from an elliptical to a more spherical shape configuration. Furthermore, cephalad fluid shifts trigger an early spaceflight diuresis, inducing a stable reduction in circulating plasma volume. To describe resulting electrophysiologic alterations and arrhythmia promotion. While most spaceflight arrhythmias are transient and non-lethal, they remain a concern for long-duration missions. Frequently reported irregularities include isolated premature atrial and ventricular complexes. Other events, including non-sustained ventricular tachycardia during spaceflight, the possibility of early-onset atrial fibrillation, and atherosclerosis in former astronauts following exposure to high-energy ionizing radiation have been documented, though the association is still being evaluated. The underlying arrhythmogenic substrate is driven by autonomic resetting, spatiotemporal heterogeneity, and QTc interval prolongation. The National Aeronautics and Space Administration utilizes a multi-faceted approach to maintain electrical stability, incorporating high-intensity interval training and electrolyte monitoring and supplementation. Real-time monitoring of wearable technology enables continuous telemetry of the heart. Recently, automated chest compression devices have been shown to significantly outperform manual cardiopulmonary resuscitation in microgravity environments. Although structural changes typically revert to baseline upon return to Earth gravity, deep-space missions present some risks. Astronauts exposed to ionizing radiation beyond Earth's magnetic field may face risk of long-term cardiovascular disease. Design of personalized nutrition to mitigate electrolyte loss and development of advanced screening tools for cardiac risk assessment are essential to improve the safety of future planetary missions.

papers.title: Effects of environmental enrichment and social isolation in preclinical rodent models: role of the endocannabinoid system.
papers.abstract: Environmental enrichment (EE) and social isolation (SI) represent contrasting forms of environmental manipulation that differentially engage homeostatic mechanisms and exert profound effects on brain function, behaviour, and health. Both EE and SI have been shown to modulate the endocannabinoid (EC) system, a key lipid signalling system involved in maintaining homeostasis and regulating diverse physiological and pathological processes. This review provides an overview of preclinical animal studies investigating the role of the EC system in the effects of EE and SI. The available evidence indicates that both EE and SI significantly alter EC signalling, with EE most commonly associated with increased CB1 receptor expression, whereas SI is associated with disrupted CB1 receptor functionality and dysregulated EC signalling. These effects are region-specific, influenced by the type and duration of environmental manipulation, developmental stage, underlying pathology and possibly sex. Pharmacological and genetic manipulation studies further implicate CB1 receptor signalling in mediating some of the beneficial effects of EE and reduced CB1 signalling in the detrimental consequences of SI on behaviour. Overall, the findings support a role for the EC system as an important mediator through which EE and SI modulate neural plasticity and behavioural outcomes. Further mechanistic and translational studies, including both sexes and relevant disease models, are needed to determine how these mechanisms may inform future prevention and treatment strategies.

papers.title: Elevated neuronal excitability and seizure susceptibility in a mouse model of SCN2A-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.
papers.abstract: Pathogenic variants in SCN2A cause a spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders, including developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEE). The patient-associated SCN2A-p.E430A variant selectively shifts voltage-dependence of activation, a mechanism predicted to enhance neuronal excitability. To investigate the functional consequences of the SCN2A-E430A variant, we generated the novel Scn2aE430A mouse model and assessed neuronal excitability, brain activity, seizure susceptibility, and phenytoin responsiveness. Heterozygous Scn2aE430A mice retained normal Scn2a expression levels and did not exhibit premature lethality. Hippocampal pyramidal neurons from heterozygous Scn2aE430A mice were hyperexcitable compared to wild-type neurons. Enhanced long-term potentiation was observed in the CA1 circuit of Scn2aE430A mice. Video-EEG data revealed recurrent epileptiform discharges and spectral abnormalities, but no spontaneous generalized seizure events. In multiple seizure-induction assays, Scn2aE430A mice had no difference in latency to first seizure signs, but exhibited faster seizure generalization and more lethality compared to wild-type mice, indicating alterations in seizure propagation and/or cessation rather than seizure initiation. Pretreatment with phenytoin improved seizure outcomes across all seizure induction methods. Together, these findings demonstrate that selective disruption of Scn2a activation gating is sufficient to drive neuronal hyperexcitability and network dysfunction, establishing the Scn2aE430A mouse as pharmacologically tractable model for investigating epilepsy related phenotypes associated with SCN2A gain of function.

papers.title: Vitamin D Insufficiency as a Nutritional Stress Amplifier: An Evidence-Weighted Framework for Adaptive Reserve under Exercise and Energy-Deficit Stress.
papers.abstract: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble secosteroid whose biological activity depends on conversion of circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D into calcitriol, the active ligand of the vitamin D receptor. Although vitamin D has often been discussed as a potential ergogenic nutrient, evidence for direct performance-enhancing effects in athletes remains inconsistent. This review proposes that vitamin D insufficiency, used here as a context-dependent descriptive label for low circulating 25(OH)D rather than as a universal diagnostic category, may function as a nutritional stress amplifier that narrows adaptive reserve when mechanical, energetic, endocrine, inflammatory, and neuroendocrine stressors converge. The strongest evidence derives from the vitamin D-calcium-phosphate-PTH-FGF23 axis, through which calcitriol-VDR signaling supports mineral homeostasis, skeletal remodeling, and resilience to repetitive skeletal loading. Emerging evidence suggests intersections with skeletal muscle repair, myokine and osteokine signaling, inflammatory regulation, and tissue adaptation, although athlete-specific validation is needed. Low energy availability and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport provide a translational model in which low circulating 25(OH)D may become more relevant because multiple nutritional, endocrine, skeletal, and recovery stressors coexist. Brain-related pathways involving fatigue, sleep, HPA-axis-related recovery, BDNF, monoaminergic signaling, and interoceptive processing are retained only as hypothesis-generating domains, not as evidence that vitamin D status modifies cognition, mood, motivation, behavior, or central recovery mechanisms in athletes. Future studies should move beyond static 25-hydroxyvitamin D assessment and unstratified supplementation trials toward dynamic stress-recovery phenotyping. This framework positions low circulating 25(OH)D status as a testable conditional modifier of stress-recovery trajectories rather than an isolated determinant of athletic performance or a primary clinical target.

papers.title: Cortical evoked potentials from deep brain stimulation of the superolateral medial forebrain bundle: An exploratory study.
papers.abstract: Deep brain stimulation of the superolateral branch of the medial forebrain bundle (slMFB-DBS) has shown promising therapeutic effects in treatment-resistant depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder. Here, we explore for the first time the electrophysiological connectivity between the stimulation target and cortical sites in humans. Electrophysiological responses to single slMFB-DBS pulses were mapped in 7 patients using epidural electrocorticography (ECoG; n = 4) or high-density electroencephalography (EEG; n = 3) over 11 sessions. Electrooculography (EOG) was simultaneously recorded, given that oculomotor side-effects are common after slMFB-DBS. Cortical evoked potentials were observed in 5 of 7 patients, with consistent latencies across modalities and prefrontal EEG topographies. In one patient, screening a broad parameter space demonstrated clear modulation of ECoG responses by DBS parameters. EOG activity consistent with oculomotor nerve co-activation was present in 6 of 7 patients, yet differed in timing and morphology from cortical responses. This work shows effective connectivity between the slMFB-DBS target and the prefrontal cortex via ECoG and EEG, complementing existing structural connectivity data. This is the first exploratory study demonstrating electrophysiological connectivity between the slMFB-DBS target and the prefrontal cortex in humans, opening the door to future studies which should systematically address their robustness and suitability for objective, biomarker-guided slMFB-DBS.

papers.title: Predictors of falls among robust community-dwelling older adults: a prospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Falls and their consequent injuries represent a threat to active aging, independence, and well-being, with critical impacts on older adults, families, and society. To investigate predictors of falls among robust community-dwelling older adults. This was a prospective cohort study in which the primary outcome was the incidence of falls during a one-year follow-up. Older adults (≥ 65 years) classified as robust according to the Clinical-Functional Vulnerability Index-20 (IVCF-20) and living in the community were included. Sociodemographic and clinical data were collected, and participants were assessed using the Timed Up and Go Test (TUG), Activities-specific Balance Confidence Scale (ABC), Falls Behavioral Scale for the Elderly (FaB-Brazil), Montreal Cognitive Assessment Basic (MoCA-B), handgrip strength test, and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). The log-rank test and multivariate Cox regression model were used for statistical analysis. A total of 94 robust older adults were included, most of whom were women (74.5%) with a mean age of 71.2 ± 4.7 years. The incidence of falls was 28.7%. In the multivariate model, a previous history of COVID-19 infection (HR = 4.30; 95% CI: 1.55-12.61; p = 0.006) and higher clinical-functional vulnerability (HR = 1.30; 95% CI: 1.02-1.70; p = 0.043) were significantly associated with the incidence of falls. Even among robust older adults, the incidence of falls was substantial. These findings reinforce the importance of screening for clinical-functional vulnerability and maintaining post-COVID-19 monitoring strategies to prevent falls in this population.

papers.title: Affective burden and resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in sleep-severity-matched chronic insomnia.
papers.abstract: Clinical heterogeneity in chronic insomnia disorder may partly reflect affective symptom burden, but its neurophysiological correlates are difficult to distinguish from those of insomnia severity. We examined whether resting-state electroencephalographic microstate dynamics differed between affective-burden phenotypes with comparable subjective sleep severity. Among 125 treatment-naive adults with chronic insomnia disorder, 21 pairs (n = 42) with low versus high affective burden, defined using prespecified Hamilton Anxiety and Depression Rating Scale thresholds, were matched 1:1 on standardized Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and Insomnia Severity Index scores. Resting-state electroencephalographic microstate features were compared between groups using linear models adjusted for residual subjective sleep severity. Further exploratory analyses of eyes-open features examined symptom associations and full-cohort dimensional associations, and evaluated classification using leave-one-pair-out cross-validation. During eyes-open rest, the high-affective-burden phenotype showed greater microstate C coverage and lower microstate D coverage, occurrence, and duration. Microstate C coverage correlated positively with a composite affective score, whereas microstate D occurrence correlated negatively with anxiety, depression, and composite affective scores. Eyes-closed analyses showed a similar trend, but the differences did not reach statistical significance. A four-feature linear support vector classifier yielded a cross-validated area under the curve of 74.8%. Corresponding effects were directionally concordant but attenuated to non-significance in full-cohort dimensional models. Although limited by the small matched sample and reliance on questionnaire-based sleep severity without objective sleep monitoring, these findings suggest that C/D microstate dynamics may be associated with affective heterogeneity in chronic insomnia. This potential association warrants further investigation in larger cohorts incorporating objective sleep measures, while the exploratory classification findings require independent external validation.

papers.title: Evaluating the frequency of conspecific pecking and foraging behaviors in two genetic strains of turkey toms with or without environmental enrichment.
papers.abstract: Conspecific pecking in turkeys can indicate unfilled behavioral and physiological needs and risk injuries to birds. Environmental enrichment has mixed success in mitigating and redirecting pecking behavior. We aimed to assess how a hanging jute rope affected the frequencies of conspecific pecking and foraging behaviors, production performance, and mortality in two commercial Large White genetic strains. Turkey toms (N = 1,056) from two strains (A and B) were randomly assigned to pens on day of hatch (22 birds/pen, 24 pens/strain). At 5 wk, a hanging jute rope was added to half of the pens (n = 12 pens/strain/enrichment treatment, CON or ROPE). Body weight (BW), body weight gain (BWG), feed intake (FI), and feed conversion ratio (FCR) were collected at 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, and 19 wk. Cumulative mortality and pecking-related culls were summarized. Video recordings at 4 and 18 wk (n = 6 pens/strain/enrichment treatment) were analyzed for 20 min in the morning and afternoon for the number of pecks directed at head/neck (HN) and back/wings/tail (BWT) and foraging bouts. Rope pecking was evaluated at 5, 8, 11, 14, and 18 wk. Turkeys pecked at the rope throughout rearing, but ROPE did not affect the frequencies of any of the behaviors, production metrics, mortality, or pecking-related culls (p > 0.05). Strain A turkeys had heavier BW, faster BWG, and higher FI than strain B turkeys throughout most of the trial (p ≤ 0.05). Strain A turkeys also performed more HN pecking at 4 and 18 wk (p < 0.001), more BWT pecking at 4 wk (p = 0.015), and more rope pecking at 8, 11, and 18 wk (p = 0.008) than strain B. Turkeys performed more BWT pecking (p < 0.001) and more foraging (p = 0.033) in the afternoon at 4 wk, while HN pecking was similar across the day (p > 0.05). The ROPE did not mitigate conspecific pecking, possibly due to loss of novelty or lack of complexity. However, insights about the relationships between conspecific pecking frequencies and genetic strain, age, and time of day could inform more effective enrichment strategies.

papers.title: Incidence and predictors of hospital readmission following paediatric tonsillectomy in a low-resource setting: A multicentre observational study.
papers.abstract: Post-tonsillectomy readmission is an important indicator of paediatric surgical safety, but evidence from resource-limited settings remains limited. This study investigated the rates and clinical predictors of readmission in Libya. These findings establish critical perioperative quality indicators to inform local discharge strategies and improve surgical safety in fragile health systems. A prospective multicentre observational study was conducted in five Libyan hospitals between 15 August 2025 and 1 August 2026. Children undergoing tonsillectomy, with or without concurrent procedures, were followed for 30 days after discharge through outpatient visits and structured telephone interviews. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, operative, and postoperative data were collected. Associations with readmission were assessed using non-parametric tests, followed by binary logistic regression. Among 291 children, the median age was 7 years (interquartile range, 5-10), and 169 (58.1%) were female. Twenty-seven patients were readmitted within 30 days, giving a readmission rate of 9.3%. Postoperative haemorrhage was the most common cause of readmission (13 patients, 48.1% of readmitted cases), followed by poor oral intake (11 patients, 40.7% of readmitted cases). Male sex was associated with increased odds of readmission (odds ratio, 3.96; 95% CI, 1.59-9.89; P = 0.003), as was recurrent tonsillitis compared with obstructive sleep disordered breathing (odds ratio, 3.54; 95% CI, 1.37-9.11; P = 0.009). Dual analgesia was associated with lower odds of readmission (odds ratio, 0.23; 95% CI, 0.06-0.84; P = 0.02). The 30-day readmission rate was 9.3%. Haemorrhage and poor oral intake were the leading causes. Male sex and recurrent tonsillitis were associated with increased odds of readmission, whereas dual-agent postoperative analgesia was associated with a reduced readmission risk. Evaluating these clinical patterns may help inform risk stratification and guide post-discharge strategies in similar clinical settings. Larger studies with standardised outcome assessment and centre-adjusted analyses are warranted.

papers.title: Physiological insights and clinical evidence of high flow nasal cannula as first-line therapy for acute hypercapnic exacerbation of COPD: a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a common lung disease. Acute exacerbations (AECOPD) are associated with increased hospitalisations and mortality. Current guidelines provide only conditional recommendation for the use of High Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC) supported by low-certainty evidence in hypercapnic respiratory failure. Since then, additional studies have been published, and we aimed to review the available literature on HFNC as a first-line therapy in hypercapnic AECOPD. Structured literature research was performed in PubMed and Embase to include studies assessing HFNC as a first-line therapy in hypercapnic AECOPD and focusing on clinical outcomes (dyspnoea, blood gas, treatment failure, mortality). Studies were categorized as single-arm studies, comparisons with conventional oxygen therapy (COT), or comparisons with non-invasive ventilation (NIV). Among 17 articles included, 2 were uncontrolled, 3 articles compared HFNC to COT and 12 compared HFNC to NIV. HFNC was often associated with better comfort and tolerance. Compared to COT, HFNC might reduce treatment failure, but evidence is still scarce. Compared to NIV, HFNC had similar effects on dyspnoea and blood gas analysis in most studies, but it remains uncertain considering treatment failure. In hypercapnic AECOPD, HFNC remains an alternative therapeutic option as compared to COT but also to NIV when the latter is contraindicated, not tolerated or during breaks from NIV. Further research is warranted with well-designed RCT focusing on treatment failure and mortality. In the future, patients might be selected considering some endotypes of AECOPD such as bronchorrhea, sleep apnea overlap or disproportionate dyspnoea which could benefit differently from HFNC.

papers.title: Valence and expectation effects shape event-related potentials to probabilistic social-evaluative feedback from putative peers.
papers.abstract: In everyday life, we receive social evaluative feedback from specific interaction partners that shapes our expectations about future feedback. It has been proposed that feedback processing and expectations are biased toward positive social feedback. However, the neuronal processes underlying biased social feedback processing remain unclear. In the current Event-Related Potentials (ERPs) study, we exposed participants to seemingly real social evaluations from three senders, each providing dichotomous positive or negative feedback on trait adjectives. In reality, feedback contingencies were manipulated with different ratios of positive versus negative feedback (rare 20 vs 80; equal 50 vs 50; frequent 80 vs 20 per cent of all trials). Participants' expectation ratings followed the general feedback ratios, though they indicated higher expectations for positive feedback. A lower probability of feedback increased all investigated ERP components, except the P1. Furthermore, positive versus negative feedback led to relatively more positive amplitudes in the Feedback-Related Negativity (FRN) and Late Positive Potential (LPP) time windows. Interactions between valence and probability were found for exploratory analyses of the Early Posterior Negativity (EPN) and theory-driven analyses of the P3, with specifically increased amplitudes for rare negative feedback compared to rare positive feedback. The results suggest that, even though negative feedback elicited higher prediction-error-related effects in ERPs associated with general surprise responses (P3) and perceptual attentional enhancement (EPN), the LPP, which is related to elaborate processing, integration, and updating, exhibited larger amplitudes for positive feedback, possibly reflecting biased processing of positive feedback. This may be fundamental for maintaining a positively biased self-view.

papers.title: The Effect of Bipolar Disorder Illness Course on Physiological Digital Signals: Observational Study.
papers.abstract: Although bipolar disorder (BD) lacks objective biomarkers of illness progression, wearable devices enable continuous, real-world collection of physiological digital biosignals, offering a promising approach to address this gap. Measures such as electrodermal activity (EDA) and heart rate variability (HRV) fluctuate with mood state and symptom severity. Previous studies have reported reduced EDA during depressive episodes and increased HRV following symptom resolution after acute mood episodes. Furthermore, greater illness burden in BD has been associated with lower HRV, suggesting that digital biosignals may capture not only state-related changes but also aspects of illness course. This study investigated whether naturalistic EDA and heart rate (HR) profiles differ according to illness course variables in BD-including diagnosis, predominant polarity, years since onset, and lifetime number of episodes-in euthymic patients, to evaluate their potential as illness course biomarkers. This cross-sectional post hoc analysis used data from 80 euthymic patients on the BD spectrum from the INTREPIBD-TIMEBASE cohort. Participants were recruited at Hospital Clínic de Barcelona (Spain) between 2021 and 2024 and wore an Empatica E4 wristband for 48 hours in naturalistic settings. Inclusion criteria comprised a current or past DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition) diagnosis of BD confirmed by structured interview and sustained euthymia. We examined the effects of 4 illness course variables (diagnosis, predominant polarity, years since onset, and number of lifetime episodes) on 3 biosignals (mean EDA, EDA peaks per minute, and HR) using generalized additive models. Interactions between illness course variables and circadian patterns were also assessed. All models were adjusted for age, sex, and current antipsychotic use and included a participant-specific random effect. Of the 80 participants, 49 (61.3%) were female; participants' mean age was 46.9 (SD 14.1) years. After adjustment for covariates and multiple comparisons, no significant associations were observed between illness course variables and EDA or HR. In sensitivity analyses excluding patients with schizoaffective disorder (n=75), years since illness onset and predominant polarity were associated with EDA peaks per minute after multiple comparison correction. Specifically, patients with more than 22 years since illness onset had fewer EDA peaks compared with other groups (β=-1.06, 95% CI -1.71 to -0.41; P=.001). No significant interactions were found between illness course variables and circadian patterns of EDA or HR. To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the association between illness course variables and EDA and HR recorded in naturalistic settings in BD. In contrast to prior findings linking illness burden with HRV, our results suggest that years since illness onset may show modest associations with phasic EDA activity. These findings indicate that digital biosignals may be more sensitive to state-related changes than to illness course characteristics, limiting their use as longitudinal biomarkers of disease progression.

papers.title: Infant bed-sharing in U.S. families: A systematic review of motivations and intervention adequacy.
papers.abstract: Over 60% of U.S. families bedshare despite knowing American Academy of Pediatrics safe sleep guidelines prohibit it. Providers and researchers have frequently attributed bed-sharing among non-white U.S. families to cultural preference, a framing that obscures structural drivers and underscores the need for more rigorous investigation of bed-sharing motivations. Among U.S. families, this systematic review identifies motivations for infant bed-sharing, with particular attention to racial and ethnic minoritized families, and evaluates whether existing interventions address these motivations. We searched CINAHL, Web of Science, PubMed, and PsychINFO for U.S. studies published since 2015 including the following topics: infants, reasons for bed-sharing, and interventions modifying bed-sharing practices. Eleven studies identifying reasons for bed-sharing and 10 intervention studies met inclusion criteria. Perceived infant safety and monitoring was the most endorsed bed-sharing reason. Current interventions show modest short-term effects, but leave complex, multifactorial motivations underlying bed-sharing unaddressed. The routine clinical attribution of bed-sharing to cultural background in the U.S. is not empirically supported and may introduce racial bias and misdirect intervention efforts. Future interventions must be culturally grounded, motivation-matched, equity-centered, and responsive to practical caregiving realities, including fatigue-driven bed-sharing, while being evaluated over clinically meaningful time horizons to reduce infant sleep-related deaths.

papers.title: Augmented reality paradigm and EA-DGCNN decoding algorithm for motor imagery in stroke patients.
papers.abstract: Stroke represents one of the leading causes of long-term motor dysfunction on a global scale. Existing motor imagery (MI) brain-computer interface (BCI) rehabilitation training systems face critical challenges of suboptimal patient engagement and limited electroencephalography (EEG) feature decoding capacity. To overcome these challenges, this study presents two primary original contributions: an independently designed wearable augmented reality (AR) MI training paradigm and a novel Euclidean Alignment-based Dynamic Graph Convolutional Neural Network (EA-DGCNN) end-to-end decoding architecture. The immersive AR-MI paradigm heightens patient engagement and enhances MI performance. The EA-DGCNN model incorporates Euclidean alignment to minimize inter-subject variability in EEG distributions. The model extracts multi-dimensional spatiotemporal features via convolutional block attention, dynamic graph attention, and multi-scale convolutions, incorporating a Broad Learning System to achieve precise classification results. Experimental results demonstrate that the model achieves an accuracy of 85.13 ± 10.53% on the public BCI Competition IV 2a dataset. On a custom clinical dataset of 20 stroke patients, the AR paradigm yields a classification accuracy of 71.9 ± 8.9%, outperforming the 68.9 ± 8.0% of the traditional 2D paradigm. Furthermore, evaluations on the 64-channel PhysioNet benchmark demonstrate robust cross-subject transferability with a superior grand-average accuracy of 83.67 ± 8.52%. Neurophysiological feature analysis indicates that the AR paradigm elicits more pronounced event-related desynchronisation and event-related synchronisation responses. The t-SNE visualisation demonstrates that the AR paradigm, coupled with the proposed model, produces highly discriminative feature clustering patterns. This study delivers a more effective paradigm and a robust decoding solution for clinical BCI rehabilitation.

papers.title: Decoding sequence auditory expectations for clinical diagnostic and prognostic assessment of prolonged disorders of consciousness.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalogram (EEG) features are important objective markers for diagnostic and prognostic evaluation of prolonged disorders of consciousness (DOC). However, task-based EEG paradigms are limited by mismatches between task demands and patients' residual awareness, as well as the limited individual assessment capacity of machine-learning-based detection frameworks. In this study, we proposed a lowdemand DOC detection strategy by decoding expectations of global regularities in sequence auditory stimulation using a modified local-global paradigm. Three single-trial classification frameworks using canonical correlation analysis, principal component analysis, and xDAWN for feature extraction were developed for individualized detection of global-regularity expectations. We further established awareness evaluation criteria based on single-trial classification outcomes and evaluated their diagnostic and prognostic effectiveness in a DOC experiment. Experiments in healthy participants demonstrated that the principal components of event-related potentials associated with global regularities were preserved under the proposed detection strategy. Compared with the original local-global paradigm, this strategy significantly improved single-trial classification performance for global effects by up to 15%. Electrophysiological analyses indicated that this improvement was driven by larger EEG response differences for global effects and more stable trial-to-trial neural states. In a cohort of 20 DOC patients, the proposed evaluation criteria achieved an individual diagnostic balanced accuracy of 68.8% (sensitivity = 50%; specificity = 87.5%), and a prognostic balanced accuracy of 60.5% (sensitivity = 50%; specificity = 71%). papers.title: Sleep, Safety and Social Media: A Qualitative Analysis of Online Discussions About Infant Sleep.
papers.abstract: Family norms, values, cultural caregiving expectations and social support can affect infant sleep practices. Evidence-based infant safe sleep recommendations are an important component of strategies to reduce the risk of sudden, unexpected infant death. This study explored how infant sleep practices were discussed across three online parenting platforms and how safe sleep guidance was discussed and represented within these conversations. Qualitative secondary data (119 posts and 525 responses) were purposively extracted from open threads on Reddit, Mumsnet and Netmums using a predefined sleep-related keyword framework informed by contemporary safe sleep guidance. Inductive thematic analysis was used to identify and develop themes and sub-themes within the discussions, followed by content and frequency analyses to quantify the occurrence of identified themes, question types and response types. Key themes included sleep behaviours, sleeping conditions and competing priorities, highlighting tensions between safe sleep recommendations and parents' practical, emotional and contextual caregiving needs. Practical advice and shared experiences were the predominant response types, while expressions of solidarity provided emotional reassurance. References to formal safe sleep guidance were limited, with parents frequently drawing on peer advice and lived experience when discussing infant sleep. The findings highlight the role of online peer support in providing spaces where parents discuss and interpret infant sleep practices and suggest the importance of understanding how safe sleep recommendations are discussed and contextualized within peer-led digital environments. This may inform more effective digital health communication that acknowledges lived parenting realities while supporting safe sleep practices and trust in health communication.

papers.title: Time-of-Day of Initial Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Administration and Its Impact on Outcomes in Metastatic Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are integral to first-line treatment of metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Circadian biology may influence antitumor immunity, raising the hypothesis that time-of-day of ICI administration could affect outcomes. We evaluated the association between initial and cumulative ICI administration time-of-day and clinical outcomes in metastatic NSCLC. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 778 patients with metastatic NSCLC treated with first-line ICI-containing therapy across Mayo Clinic sites between January 2021 and March 2024. Patients were stratified by time-of-day of first ICI administration: early (0700-1200) versus late (1201-2400). Primary end points were overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS); the secondary end point was immune-related toxicity. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for clinically relevant covariates. Exploratory analyses evaluated cumulative infusion time-of-day and alternative administration-time thresholds using spline and cut-point analyses. Of 778 patients, 277 received early and 501 received late initial ICI administration. Median OS was 1.33 versus 1.48 versus years and median PFS was 0.65 versus 0.67 years in the late and early groups, respectively. Time-of-day of initial ICI administration was not associated with OS (HR, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.85 to 1.20]) or PFS (HR, 1.03 [95% CI, 0.88 to 1.21]). Findings were unchanged after multivariable adjustment. Immune-related toxicity occurred in 26.9% and 24.2% of patients in the late and early groups, respectively (P = .40). Cumulative infusion time-of-day was not associated with OS or PFS, and spline analyses identified no significant administration-time threshold associated with outcomes. In this large real-world cohort of patients with metastatic NSCLC, neither initial nor cumulative ICI administration time-of-day was associated with survival or immune-related toxicity. Prospective studies incorporating chronotype and circadian biomarkers are warranted to further define the role of chronotherapy in immuno-oncology.

papers.title: Use of Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation for Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Adults With Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities.
papers.abstract: The objective of this study was to assess the safety, efficacy, and patient satisfaction of hypoglossal nerve stimulation (HNS) therapy as an alternative to continuous positive airway pressure therapy for obstructive sleep apnea in adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDDs), including trisomy 21 and cerebral palsy. We conducted an observational study of 4 adults with IDDs and moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea who underwent implantation of an HNS device. Patient demographic characteristics, device usage, obstructive sleep apnea and daytime sleepiness outcomes, and patient satisfaction scores were retrospectively reviewed and analyzed. The mean adherence rate was 92.3%. The mean [SD] pretreatment apnea-hypopnea index was 39.0 [16.7] events per hour, which decreased to 8.5 [4.7] event per hour after treatment, representing a mean [SD] reduction of 77.5% [12.9%]. Epworth Sleepiness Scale scores decreased in 2 patients, were unchanged in 1 patient, and increased in 1 patient. Patient-reported satisfaction was high, with mean [SD] scores of 5.0 [0.0] for comfort, ease of deactivation, and effectiveness and 4.5 [0.6] for ease of activation. Treatment of obstructive sleep apnea with HNS was associated with decreased apnea-hypopnea index values and was well tolerated among adults with IDDs, suggesting that it may be a viable alternative to continuous positive airway pressure therapy for patients who cannot tolerate conventional treatment. However, the variable Epworth Sleepiness Scale findings and small sample highlight the need for larger studies with long-term follow-up to further evaluate the safety and effectiveness of HNS in this population.

papers.title: In Sync with the Kidney: Reciprocal Regulation of Renal Circadian Rhythms.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms regulate the time of day at which various physiological processes take place, including the functions of the kidney. This regulation is made possible by key transcriptional regulators: the core molecular circadian clock, which mediates expression of clock-controlled genes on a 24-h cycle. The present landscape of circadian rhythm research in the kidney spans impacts on the clinical level as well as in basic research, where its role in individual kidney cell types, disease states, and the impacts of environmental stressors is being studied. Recent research has also identified sex differences, cross talk between various tissues, and immune signaling as important considerations for understanding the circadian clocks within the kidney. This review synthesizes the current knowledge of circadian rhythms of the kidney in regard to these issues and stresses the importance of time of day in research as well as in patient health.

Saccadic suppression enhances saliency of ecologically relevant stimuli in the zebrafish optic tectum.
papers.abstract: Saccadic suppression, a reduction in visual sensitivity around the time of rapid eye movements, is well-documented in primate psychophysics, but its mechanisms and functions remain debated. Here, we use zebrafish to trace the origins of saccadic suppression, and we demonstrate how saccadic suppression selectively enhances the visual salience of ecologically relevant stimuli. Saccadic suppression thus contributes to more than just compensation for rapid saccade-induced image shifts. We first established a behavioral correlate of saccadic suppression in larval zebrafish escape behavior. Then, using electrophysiology, we show that retinal ganglion cells jumpstart saccadic suppression in a spatial frequency-dependent manner. Calcium imaging, combined with 360° visual stimulation and behavioral tracking, revealed that motor signals enhance peri-saccadic suppression strength in the optic tectum, where suppression lasts for more than 3,000 ms. Notably, saccadic suppression is much weaker and more short-lived for stimuli related to hunting or escape behavior than for behaviorally less relevant global flashes. This unequal attenuation effectively increases the salience of the ecologically relevant stimuli in the optic tectum after saccades. Our results demonstrate that saccadic suppression integrates visual and motor signals to optimize sensory processing within neural constraints, and they provide insights into evolutionarily conserved visual strategies.

papers.title: A high robustness decoding technique for ultrasound modulated electroencephalogram.
papers.abstract: Ultrasound-modulated electroencephalography (USMEEG) has become a vital tool in neuroscience because it integrates millimeter-level spatial resolution with millisecond-level temporal resolution. However, under extremely complex scenarios, excessively strong or weak acoustoelectric signal coupling leads to severe distortion in USMEEG decoded signals. To address this, we developed a highly robust decoding algorithm based on the ultrasound pulse repetition frequency and introduced the acoustoelectric modulation ratio (AMR) to quantify different modulation scenarios. Across numerical simulations, phantoms, and validation using human steady-state visual evoked potential signals with data-level acoustoelectric coupling across 10 volunteers, the focused ultrasound phased array achieved an encoding spatial resolution of 0.79 millimeters. The proposed algorithm significantly outperformed four traditional methods, exhibiting higher precision under weak modulation (0 < AMR ≤ 0.6), moderate modulation (0.6 < AMR ≤ 1), and over modulation (AMR > 1) conditions, with average decoding correlations reaching 0.84, 0.90, and 0.89. This highly robust technique expands USMEEG applications and provides a technical foundation for high-performance noninvasive brain-computer interfaces.

papers.title: Environmental enrichment is associated with changes in the gut microbiome and resistome of captive pythons.
papers.abstract: Environmental enrichment is widely used to improve the welfare of captive animals, yet its effects on reptilian gut microbiota remain poorly understood. Here, we used shotgun metagenomic sequencing to investigate the gut microbiome and resistome of two captive python species: Burmese python (Python bivittatus) and reticulated python (Malayopython reticulatus), before and after environmental enrichment. We found that environmental enrichment was associated with increased α-diversity in Burmese pythons, as indicated by significantly higher ACE and observed species indices, while NMDS ordination revealed differences in the observed patterns of community composition between the two species. Pseudomonadota and Bacteroidota were dominant phyla in the gut microbiota of both python species, but their relative abundances responded differently to enrichment between hosts. Functional analyses suggested an enhanced metabolic potential in Burmese pythons, particularly in carbohydrate metabolism and environmental information processing, accompanied by increased abundance of carbohydrate-active enzymes. In addition, enrichment may influence the gut resistome, with Pseudomonadota contributing the majority of antibiotic resistance genes. Overall, our results demonstrate that environmental enrichment measures, such as dietary changes and improvements in water and air quality, are associated with changes in the gut microbiome and resistome of captive pythons in a host-dependent manner, highlighting the combined roles of diet and environmental conditions in the observed changes in the gut microbiota. These findings provide exploratory insights into the functional responses and host-microbiome evolution of reptile gut microbiota to captivity and have important implications for the management and welfare of captive animals.

papers.title: A three process approach for insomnia-like awakenings.
papers.abstract: Mathematical modelling of sleep is a growing field, with an increasing number of applications to sleep disorders. However, despite its high prevalence and under-diagnosis worldwide, insomnia has not been among these disorders. We chart the development of sleep models and investigate the hypothesis that they can be simply modified to model insomnia, ultimately introducing a new model focusing on nocturnal awakenings as a starting point of insomnia-like behaviour, based on a three process approach. We find that several of these models can make promising steps towards producing nighttime awakenings characteristic of many types of insomnia with minor modifications, but that none can fully reproduce every key criterion with only minor adaptations. In particular, we find that the stability of the sleeping state is an important factor in more complex contemporary neuronal population models' abilities to incorporate awakenings, with both permanently stable and permanently non-stable sleep proving to be obstacles. Instead, we base our new model on the simpler foundational two process model, incorporating an original, quantitative wakefulness drive. We further analyse the sensitivity of its new parameters and the statistical properties of the nighttime awakening phenomena it produces. This new drive includes both physiology-based arousal impulses and environmental and psychological disturbances, and provides the foundation of a new approach to future quantitative modelling of insomnia phenotypes.

papers.title: Expression of Concern: Epidemiological studies of sleep disorder in educational community of Pakistani population, its major risk factors and associated diseases.
Dynamic cortical connectivity underlying proprioceptive processing during NMES-induced hand movements: Insights from an acute deafferentation model.
papers.abstract: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) is a promising modality for restoring sensory feedback in upper-limb prosthetics. However, the dynamic cortical mechanisms underlying the perception of NMES-evoked muscle contraction, particularly under conditions of sensory loss (e.g., amputation), remain poorly understood. This study investigates the time-varying effective connectivity of the sensorimotor cortex in response to NMES using the ischemic nerve block (INB) technology to model acute deafferentation. 64-channel EEG data were recorded from 11 able-bodied participants under a 2×2 factorial design involving INB states (before vs. block) and stimulation intensities (above vs. below motor threshold). The adaptive directed transfer function (ADTF) combined with graph theoretical analysis was employed to quantify dynamic causal interactions in the Beta band (15-30 Hz). The NMES-evoked cortical response progressed through three stages with monotonically increasing network segregation and integration (PFDR ≤ 0.01 for all stage-wise comparisons). During the ischemic nerve block (INB), the clustering coefficient (CC) and global efficiency (Ge) decreased under above-threshold stimulation (cluster-level PFDR = 0.019 and PFDR = 0.013, respectively), whereas below-threshold stimulation elicited a transient CC increase (150-525 ms, PFDR = 0.019) followed by late Ge reductions. The differentiation of the network response between above and below motor-threshold stimulation was reconfigured rather than abolished during deafferentation. At the regional level, deafferentation attenuated contralateral somatosensory and ipsilateral motor driving, whereas ipsilateral somatosensory outflow was relatively enhanced. NMES-evoked muscle contractions modulate the dynamics of sensorimotor networks by acute deafferentation. Acute deafferentation attenuates network integration and increases the relative contribution of the ipsilateral hemisphere. These electrophysiological markers may inform the design and evaluation of closed-loop sensory feedback for neuroprostheses.

papers.title: Tau-driven hyperexcitability of locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons underlies sleep fragmentation and cognitive decline in mice.
papers.abstract: Early sleep disruption is a hallmark of preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD), but its underlying mechanisms are unclear. The locus coeruleus (LC) dopamine-β-hydroxylase noradrenergic (LCDBH) neurons are vulnerable to early tau pathology in AD. Using P301S transgenic mice and cell-type-specific tau overexpression models, we show that pathological tau accumulation selectively increases the intrinsic excitability of LCDBH neurons. Tau-induced neuronal hyperactivity disrupts sleep homeostasis, reduces non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and slow-wave activity, increases sleep fragmentation and microarousals, and delays both anesthetic induction and sleep onset. Furthermore, tau overexpression in LCDBH neurons leads to significant recognition memory deficits. Notably, optogenetic suppression of LCDBH-tau neuronal activity reverses sleep disturbances and rescues cognitive dysfunction. Our findings demonstrate that tau-driven hyperexcitability of LCDBH neurons is a core driver of early sleep and cognitive impairments in AD, providing a mechanistic insight and potential target for preclinical AD treatment.

papers.title: Cannabidiol and fronto-parietal EEG connectivity in autistic children.
papers.abstract: Autistic children often show altered brain network connectivity, including circuitry implicated in social cognition. Cannabidiol (CBD) has emerged as a potential therapy for autism, but its neural mechanisms remain under-researched. Here, we analyze resting-state data collected as part of a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial, to explore whether 12 weeks of oral CBD oil could modulate functional connectivity in autistic children. Twenty-nine autistic children (5 to 12 years) completed two 12-week intervention periods (CBD and placebo, randomized) separated by an 8-week washout. Before and after each period, 5 min of eyes-open resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) were obtained from a subset of 18 participants (8 female). Functional connectivity was calculated across 16 electrode-pairs in the delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands. Beta-band connectivity between the right frontal and right inferior-parietal electrodes increased following CBD (P = 0.001, false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected P [pFDR] = 0.022), and alpha connectivity showed an increase that did not remain following FDR correction (P = 0.036, pFDR = 0.428). No significant differences were observed following placebo for any frequency band (pFDR > 0.69). This study provides preliminary evidence that 12 weeks of cannabidiol is associated with an increase in right fronto-parietal (F4-P8) functional connectivity in autistic children, most pronounced in the beta-band. Replication in larger samples is needed to confirm generalizability and clinical relevance.

papers.title: Electronic excited states and photodissociation pathways of iso-propylamine: Experimental and theoretical investigations.
papers.abstract: We report for the first time absorption cross sections of iso-propylamine in the energy range of 40 000 to 80 000 cm-1 using synchrotron radiation. Quantum chemical calculations based on time-dependent density functional theory are used to conduct a detailed spectral analysis. The observed intensity profile of the room temperature absorption spectrum is well reproduced by a theoretical simulation that includes vertical excitation energies and oscillator strengths of its two stable conformers, gauche (G) and anti (A). Rydberg series that converge to the first ionization limit of iso-propylamine are assigned via quantum defect analysis. Several vibronic progressions are observed along with the Rydberg series. The dominance of progressions involving the NH2 wagging mode observed along with the 3s Rydberg transition implies a molecular geometry change involving the NH2 group in the excited state. This is confirmed by geometry optimization calculations, which predict a planar geometry in the excited state vis-à-vis pyramidal geometry in the ground state. The measured absorption cross sections are used to estimate the lower limit of the UV photolysis lifetime of iso-propylamine in the upper atmosphere. In addition, the photodissociation dynamics of iso-propylamine probed using potential energy scans of S1, T1, and T2 excited states along each of the possible direct bond cleavage channels show that direct dissociation via S1 is unlikely, and intersystem crossings may play an important role. Molecular channels involving H atom migration leading to CH4 and NH3 formation in both iso-propylamine and n-propylamine are investigated and compared using intrinsic reaction coordinate calculations.

papers.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Maternal Health Outcomes in Pregnant and Postpartum Individuals: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used to support maternal health, but randomized evidence is limited. To evaluate whether access to a generative AI maternal health chatbot improved 12-month maternal health outcomes. This 2-group randomized clinical trial enrolled 400 participants from October 2023 to December 2024, with 12-month follow-up completed in December 2025. Participants were recruited online across 49 US states and the District of Columbia. Eligible participants were English-speaking, aged 14 years or older, pregnant or parenting an infant younger than 6 months, and self-identified as members of racial and/or ethnic minoritized groups. Participants were randomized 1:1 to receive access to the chatbot or an active control consisting of monthly children's books. Primary outcomes were anxiety and depression symptoms at 12 months measured using the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 and Patient Health Questionnaire-9. Secondary outcomes included emergency department visits, pregnancy-related complications, postpartum care checkups, effective contraception use, and sleep duration. Among 400 randomized participants, the mean (SD) age was 32.6 (5.1) years; 200 (50%) were parenting an infant at enrollment; and 10 (2%) identified as American Indian or Alaska Native, 80 (20%) Asian, 188 (47%) Black or African American, 57 (14%) multiracial, and 65 (16%) Hispanic or Latino. The AI chatbot was not associated with differences in anxiety scores (adjusted mean difference, 0.10; 95% CI, -0.77 to 0.96) or depression scores (adjusted mean difference, -0.23; 95% CI, -1.05 to 0.59), nor with emergency department visits, postpartum care, contraception use, or sleep duration. Among participants pregnant at enrollment, the chatbot was associated with more self-reported pregnancy-related complications in the secondary 12-month end point analysis, but not in longitudinal analyses. Higher chatbot engagement was associated with longer sleep duration and higher anxiety scores in exploratory within-group analyses. In this randomized clinical trial of pregnant and postpartum individuals from racial and ethnic minoritized groups, access to a generative artificial intelligence maternal health chatbot did not improve maternal anxiety or depression at 12 months compared with an active control. Secondary and exploratory findings should be interpreted cautiously. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06053515.

papers.title: Reduced desaturation-based detection of sleep apnea events in self-identified Black individuals across two cohorts.
papers.abstract: Pulse oximetry may overestimate oxygen saturation in individuals with darker skin pigmentation, potentially reducing detection of desaturation during sleep-disordered breathing. To assess racial/ethnic differences in desaturation-based obstructive event detection and cardiovascular risk, and evaluate heart-rate response as an oximetry-independent marker for risk stratification. We analyzed participants without cardiovascular disease in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis(MESA) and Sleep Heart Health Study(SHHS). We modeled desaturation-based AHI relative to airflow-defined AHI and examined AHI-ΔHR6, defined by respiratory events with a heart-rate increase ≥6 beats/min. Adjusted Cox models evaluated associations with a composite outcome, major adverse cardiovascular events or all-cause mortality(MACE/mortality). Black participants had 21% and 20% lower proportions of airflow-defined events meeting the ≥4% desaturation criterion than White participants in MESA (ratio 0.79[95% CI,0.68-0.93]; p = 0.003) and SHHS (0.80[0.68-0.94]; p = 0.008), respectively. No other racial/ethnic group showed a lower proportion of airflow-defined events meeting desaturation criteria than White participants. AHI-ΔHR6 event detection was similar between Black and White participants in both cohorts. In Whites participants, desaturation-based events were associated with MACE/mortality in MESA but not in SHHS, while desaturation-based AHI measures were not significantly associated with MACE/mortality in Black individuals in either cohort. In contrast, AHI-ΔHR6 was associated with MACE/mortality in MESA (HR 1.33[1.09-1.63];p=0.006) and SHHS (1.26[1.02-1.55]; p = 0.033). Desaturation-based scoring identified a lower proportion of reduced flow events in Black than White participants, whereas heart-rate-response-based event detection was similar across groups, suggesting oximetry-related under-detection in individuals with darker pigment.
papers.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine

papers.title: Comprehensive classification of HCN1 variants linked to neurodevelopmental disorders with and without epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated 1 (HCN1) channels mediate the cationic Ih current, a fundamental regulator of neuronal excitability and synaptic integration, and are predominantly expressed in the cortex and hippocampus. Although HCN1 variants have been increasingly identified in patients with epilepsy, from milder forms to developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEE), genotype-phenotype correlations remain poorly defined. Here, we used patch-clamp electrophysiology and confocal imaging in HEK293 cells to functionally characterize 43 HCN1 variants identified in patients with neurodevelopmental disorders, with or without epilepsy. Based on biophysical properties, we established a classification system comprising four distinct functional classes: I) low or no current; II) hyperpolarizing shift in voltage dependence; III) depolarizing shift in voltage dependence; and IV) generation of an instantaneous current. The molecular basis for this classification was further interpreted using available cryo-EM structures of HCN1. Integration with clinical data from 50 patients revealed a striking correlation between functional class and clinical presentation. Loss-of-function variants prevailed among individuals with milder phenotypes or without epilepsy, with the latter distinctively clustering within the channel selectivity filter. In contrast, gain-of-function and mixed variants were predominantly associated with DEE. Finally, we demonstrate that allosteric modulators, including peptides NB6 and TRIP8bnano and the small molecule J&J12e, effectively normalize channel function across three of the four classes in vitro. These findings establish a biophysical framework for interpreting HCN1 variants, demonstrating that the direction of channel dysfunction is a major determinant of epilepsy risk and severity, and providing a conceptual foundation for future class-based precision medicine approaches.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

papers.title: Constructing a US Value Set for Child Health States: The PedsUtil Scoring System.
papers.abstract: The Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) is a widely used, generic, health-related quality of life instrument validated for children aged 2-18 years. However, because it is not preference weighted, it cannot be directly used to estimate health utilities for economic evaluations. This study constructed a value set for the PedsQL: the PedsUtil scoring system. Preferences for child health states were elicited from US adults using an online discrete choice experiment (n = 2518) and composite time trade-off survey (n = 868). Child health states were defined by the seven-dimension PedsUtil health state classification system previously derived from the PedsQL. Discrete choice experiment data were analyzed using a mixed logistic regression and the latent coefficients were anchored onto the quality-adjusted life year scale using composite time trade-off data with a linear mapping approach. Preferences varied with age. Pain was the most important dimension for ages 2-4 years and Social Functioning was most important for ages 5-18 years. Pairwise comparisons confirmed significant preference differences between the youngest and older age groups and these age-related differences were also reflected in composite time trade-off data. Consequently, age-specific scoring systems (2-4 and 5-18 years) and an age-combined scoring system (2-18 years) were developed. Utility ranges for the final scoring systems were 0.368-0.999 for ages 2-4 years, 0.427-0.951 for ages 5-18 years, and 0.410-0.972 for ages 2-18 years combined. The PedsUtil scoring system is the first value set derived for the PedsQL, enabling direct estimation of health utilities from PedsQL responses and facilitating pediatric economic evaluations.

papers.title: Insomnia partially mediates the association between ADHD traits and depressive symptoms in Japanese nursing students.
papers.abstract: Nursing students with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) traits may struggle with demanding academic and clinical training, potentially increasing the risk of insomnia and depressive symptoms. This study examined whether insomnia statistically mediates the association between ADHD traits and depressive symptoms in this population. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 131 nursing students (96.9% female; mean age = 20.4 ± 2.3 years) at two Japanese universities in late October-November 2018, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. Participants completed measures of ADHD traits (ASRS v1.1 Part A), depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), and insomnia (Athens Insomnia Scale). A bootstrapped mediation analysis (5,000 resamples), adjusted for age, sex, and sleep/circadian factors (sleep duration, chronotype, social jetlag), was performed. ADHD traits showed a weak positive correlation with insomnia (r = 0.29, p < 0.001) and a moderate positive correlation with depressive symptoms (r = 0.44, p < 0.001); insomnia and depressive symptoms were moderately correlated (r = 0.54, p < 0.001). Insomnia partially mediated the association between ADHD traits and depressive symptoms: the indirect effect was significant (β = 0.105, 95% bootstrap CI [0.024, 0.194]; Sobel z = 2.49, p = 0.013), accounting for approximately 26% of the total effect, while the direct effect remained significant (β = 0.293, p < 0.001). A Monte Carlo post-hoc power analysis indicated that statistical power for the indirect effect was 0.82. These findings, interpreted within the constraints of a cross-sectional design, identify insomnia as a candidate mechanism linking ADHD traits to depressive symptoms and suggest that integrating sleep health screening and targeted sleep-focused interventions into nursing education may offer a feasible and scalable preventive approach to supporting student mental health within higher-education support systems.

papers.title: From Macroenvironmental Context to Individual Proximal Exposure: Multiscale Mechanisms Linking Environmental Factors to Blood Pressure Homeostasis and Variability : Author.
papers.abstract: Hypertension is a major contributor to the global burden of cardiovascular disease. In addition to genetics, age, and lifestyle, environmental exposures can disrupt blood pressure homeostasis. Compared with air pollution and ambient temperature, evidence concerning psychosocial factors, noise, light, chemical pollutants, micro- and nanoplastics, and the individual proximal residential environment is more fragmented, and studies often conflate mean blood pressure, incident hypertension, and blood pressure variability (BPV) as equivalent outcomes. Using a continuum from macroenvironmental context to individual proximal exposure, this review integrates evidence from human studies, animal experiments, and in vitro research to compare associations of air pollution, temperature, greenspace, noise, chemical pollutants, micro- and nanoplastics, light exposure, and psychosocial stress with distinct blood pressure phenotypes. We further summarize shared pathways involving autonomic and neurohumoral regulation, oxidative stress-inflammation-endothelial injury, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), circadian rhythms, and metabolic/microbiome mechanisms. Human evidence is relatively substantial for air pollution, temperature, noise, and greenspace, whereas direct evidence linking micro- and nanoplastics and some chemical pollutants to human hypertension and BPV remains limited, with mechanistic understanding derived mainly from experimental models. Multiple exposures, genetic and epigenetic backgrounds, and socioeconomic conditions may jointly modify environmental effects. Clarifying exposure dose, level of evidence, and the relevant BPV time scale will help identify environmentally susceptible populations and provide a conceptual basis for stratified prevention and future intervention studies.

papers.title: Effects of digital stress-management interventions in breast cancer patients 18 months after intervention access.
papers.abstract: Digital stress-management tools show promise, but their long-term impact remains unclear. In the Coping After Breast Cancer (CABC) trial, the app-based stress-management program StressProffen, with either cognitive behavioral therapy intervention (CBI) or a mindfulness-based intervention (MBI), showed no advantage over usual care after six months of access. However, benefits may emerge gradually, as users need time not only to become familiar with the content and techniques, but also to internalize, apply and automatize their use in response to real-life stressors. The a priori defined aims of the current study were to examine; 1) whether extended (18 months) access to the digital stress-management interventions CBI and MBI were associated with changes in perceived stress (stress) (primary outcome), measures of health-related quality of life, mindfulness, fatigue, coping, anxiety, depression, and sleep (secondary outcomes), 2) association between app use and changes in stress level and investigate baseline characteristics as moderators of change in stress in the intervention groups, and 3) identify predictors of change in stress among patients with breast cancer. Of 430 patients randomized to MBI, CBI, or usual care, 76% (n = 327) completed the 18-month survey. Linear mixed-effects models were used to assess between-group differences in primary and secondary outcomes. Moderator analyses were performed to examine whether specific baseline characteristics modified the intervention effects on stress levels. Predictor analysis of change in stress was performed for the total sample. At 18 months, all three groups showed stable trends over time, with no significant difference between either intervention group and controls. A larger stress reduction was observed among younger participants (≤50 years) in both CBI and MBI compared to controls. Higher baseline stress levels predicted significantly larger stress reductions in the total sample, but the moderator analysis showed that the effects were only significant in the CBI group. Neither CBI nor MBI showed statistically significant improvements at 18 months compared to controls. The results however suggest that long-term access to stress management interventions may help young women with breast cancer and those with high initial stress to reduce their stress levels. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT04480203.

papers.title: Distinct Systemic Metabolic Remodeling and Neurobehavioral Deterioration in Chemotherapy-Treated Lung Cancer Models.
papers.abstract: Peripheral tumors and chemotherapy reshape host physiology, yet model selection for cancer-related neurobehavioral deterioration often remains empirical. In lung cancer, this deterioration often presents clinically as a somatic-psychological symptom cluster that includes fatigue, pain-related symptoms, sleep disturbance, and distress. We asked whether chemotherapy-treated subcutaneous and orthotopic Lewis lung carcinoma models reproduce a comparable symptom-related state or instead reflect distinct systemic and neurobehavioral contexts. Male C57BL/6J mice bearing subcutaneous tumors (STCG) or orthotopic tumors (OTCG), together with normal controls, were followed through chemotherapy using behavioral measures of fatigue-related performance, pain/discomfort responses, sleep-related responses, center-zone exploration and passive coping. These trajectories were interpreted alongside plasma metabolic profiles and targeted peripheral and brain pathological readouts. The two models diverged. STCG preserved survival and showed an active sickness-like pattern, including impaired rotarod performance, delayed sleep onset and a trend toward shortened thermal response latency. OTCG showed survival attrition, late-stage systemic deterioration, reduced thermal nociceptive responsiveness, prolonged pentobarbital-induced sleep duration and stronger behavioral suppression. Plasma metabolomics revealed broader remodeling in OTCG, involving ketone body, glutathione, one-carbon and redox-related pathways. Both tumor-bearing models showed peripheral oxidative stress and brain alterations involving Claudin-5, glial activation and synaptic markers. Exploratory within-model networks identified fatigue-related performance as a highly connected node, with differing behavioral and biological associations. These findings suggest that the two models capture complementary but non-interchangeable metabolic and neurobehavioral states under the tested chemotherapy conditions.
papers.journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology

papers.title: The Applied Sport Science of Professional Male Basketball: A Narrative Review of Current and Emerging Practices.
papers.abstract: Basketball is a physically demanding intermittent team sport which requires a multifaceted approach to optimise player preparation, performance, health, and recovery. Quantifying the training and match demands of professional basketball players can help practitioners develop effective strategies for managing fatigue, monitoring training loads, and guiding physical preparation. Sleep and travel disruptions present additional challenges to practitioners and can have deleterious effects on recovery and readiness to compete. Nutrition is also an essential component supporting performance and recovery and should be individualised to the needs of each player. The inherent complexity of basketball requires practitioners to develop a holistic view that considers the interaction between tactical, technical, psychological, and physical basketball-related factors along with external factors from the greater basketball system (e.g., players, coaches, support staff, organisations, schedules, referees, and governing bodies) that can influence performance. Advances in technology continue to shape performance monitoring, injury-risk forecasting, and training methodologies, yet practitioners must be aware of potential risks such as player privacy concerns and the misuse of data. A comprehensive understanding of these factors provides valuable insights for practitioners to develop effective evidence-based strategies and frameworks for working with professional male basketball players.

papers.title: Assessing the impact of menstrual cycle phase on respiration rate, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, nocturnal oxygenation and sleep time using wearable devices.
papers.abstract: BackgroundPrior studies have observed changes in parameters such as respiration rate, heart rate variability, and resting heart rate over the course of the menstrual cycle. However, prior studies have been limited in scale and have not considered concurrent variations in sleep duration or nocturnal oxygenation.ObjectivesTo determine the variations in nocturnal respiration rate, heart rate variability, resting heart, main sleep duration and average nocturnal SpO2, associated with underlying menstrual cycle timing.DesignThis was a retrospective observational study based on wearable data and self-reported menstrual cycle timing and birth control usage.MethodsData was collected over 24 months in women using wearable devices (Fitbit and Pixel Watch) who also self-recorded their menstrual cycles and birth control usage. The study considered 1754 women on hormonal birth control (HBC) pills, and 7279 naturally cycling (NC) women. Self-reported menstrual cycle parameters were consistent with normal physiology, and participants recorded wearable data on greater than 70% of the nights.ResultsBy averaging parameters relative to their day within a menstrual cycle, variations were seen in respiration rate (RR), resting heart rate (RHR) and heart rate variability (HRV), dependent on cycle phase. For the NC cohort, RR varied between the assumed follicular and luteal phase by approximately 0.6 breaths/min (∼4% variation, p<0.05), RHR by 3.0 bpm (∼4.4%, p<0.05), and HRV by 6 ms (∼14%, p<0.05). RR was highest in the assumed premenstrual phase, and lowest near the assumed ovulation date. There were also variations in main sleep time (7 minutes longer in menses than pre-menstrual, p<0.05), and in average nocturnal SpO2 (absolute increase of ∼0.1% in assumed late luteal phase, p<0.05). Similar patterns were seen in the HBC group with reduced amplitude of variation. At a cohort level, increased respiration rate was observed in the HBC group (about 0.2 breaths/min, p<0.05), as was increased main sleep time by approximately 7 minutes.ConclusionThe menstrual cycle has a small but statistically significant effect on a number of cardiorespiratory variables over a typical cycle. The effect size is largest for changes in resting heart rate, followed by HRV and respiration rate, with effects on main sleep time and SpO2 being negligible.
