For N1 stage classification which is more challenging, it reaches an accuracy of 57.5%, 52.5% and 49.3% on three datasets, respectively. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach and its certain advantages over existing methods.

papers.title: Symptom clusters and symptom network characteristics in chronic fatigue syndrome patients: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Chronic fatigue syndrome is characterized by multiple co-occurring physical, cognitive, sleep, and emotional symptoms. Traditional symptom cluster analysis identifies patterns of symptom co-occurrence but does not clarify the relative importance of individual symptoms or the connections between symptom clusters. Symptom network analysis may complement this approach by identifying core and bridge symptoms. To investigate the symptom clusters and structural characteristics of symptom networks in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome, thereby providing a basis for developing targeted strategies for managing symptoms. A convenience sampling method was used to enroll 214 patients with chronic fatigue syndrome. Data were collected using a demographic questionnaire and an adapted version of the Chinese Memorial Symptom Assessment Scale. Data were analyzed using SPSS 27.0. Symptom clusters were extracted using principal component analysis (PCA) with varimax rotation, and a symptom network was constructed in R to calculate expected influence and bridge expected influence, thereby identifying core and bridge symptoms. The three most common symptoms, in descending order, were fatigue (100.00%), difficulty concentrating (90.7%), and feeling drowsy (86.9%). A total of six symptom clusters were identified: Emotional-Sleep Symptom cluster, Fatigue Symptom cluster, Physical symptom cluster, Self-Image symptom cluster, Gastrointestinal symptom cluster, and Neurological symptom cluster, with a cumulative variance contribution of 63.114%. Fatigue had the highest expected influence (rEI = 1.541), followed by worrying (rEI = 1.169); fatigue (rbEI = 0.430), pain (rbEI = 0.363), and difficulty sleeping (rbEI = 0.309) were the primary bridge symptoms. Patients with chronic fatigue syndrome exhibit co-occurring symptoms and connections across symptom clusters. Fatigue serves as both a core symptom and a bridging symptom, while worrying, difficulty sleeping, and pain are also critical areas of focus in symptom management. Clinically, fatigue should be prioritized for assessment and management, while concurrently conducting comprehensive evaluations of mood, sleep, and pain. Individualized management plans should be developed based on the characteristics of symptom clusters and symptom networks to alleviate the symptom burden in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome and improve their quality of life.

papers.title: Mapping the technology-demand interface: how brain organoid evolution is reshaping the translational landscape of stroke.
papers.abstract: Stroke research faces a dual modeling barrier: interspecies divergence and oversimplified 2D cultures have contributed to the failure of many neuroprotective trials. Brain organoids, which provide human genetic backgrounds and 3D neural networks, offer a promising but incomplete solution. Existing reviews often address isolated technological aspects without linking them to stroke-specific demands. This narrative review establishes a "technological iteration-clinical demand" mapping matrix (Figure 1). We trace organoid evolution from static oxygen-glucose deprivation models to vascularized, assembloid, and microfluidic chip-integrated systems, and toward multi-organ coupling. We highlight how these advances may uncover human-specific neuroinflammation, proposed PANoptosis-like spatiotemporal cascades, and synaptic deficits mediated by human-specific genes such as SRGAP2C. We argue that the inability of animal models to resolve certain human-specific targets is driving organoids from static endpoint models toward dynamic platforms with perfusable vasculature and immune integration, although current systems remain at an early stage. We critically evaluate the preclinical role of organoids, defining scenarios where they may partially replace animal testing and where they cannot. Major bottlenecks include fetal-like organoid maturity (transcriptome approximately equivalent to gestational weeks 12-20) versus the average stroke onset age of about 70 years, and the absence of peripheral immune infiltration, which mediates a large fraction of secondary injury. We outline potential solutions including multi-omics integration, inducible aging, gene editing, and multi-organ chip coupling, and emphasize that standardized evaluation frameworks are needed to translate organoid findings into personalized stroke therapy.
papers.journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology

papers.title: Systemic inflammatory response index: a potential mediator between substance use disorder and sleep disturbance.
papers.abstract: Substance use disorder (SUD) and sleep disturbance share a complex, bidirectional relationship. However, the role of the systemic inflammation response index (SIRI) in this relationship remains to be explored, which will be beneficial for detecting SUD-related sleep disturbances. Utilizing diverse samples from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) (n = 2,533) as well as self-collected clinical data (n = 88), we explored the associations among SUD, SIRI, and sleep disturbance. In NHANES dataset, weighted logistic regression and multiple machine learning (ML) models were employed to assess the relationship between SIRI and sleep disturbance, as well as SIRI importance in SUD group. Mediation analysis examined the role of SIRI in mediating the SUD-sleep disturbance association. During clinical confirmation, a two-sample t-test was used to discover differences in SIRI between opioid use disorder (OUD) and healthy controls (HC). Correlation of SIRI and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) was performed by partial correlation within OUD group. The analyses on NHANES datasets uncovered significant "SUD-SIRI-sleep disturbance" relationships, and SIRI ranked first in diagnosing sleep status of SUD subjects. Through validation via clinical datasets, OUD individuals also had higher SIRI levels and sleep disturbance risk than HC. Our findings suggest that SIRI statistically mediates the relationship between SUD and sleep disturbance in a cross-sectional context, positioning it as a potential adjunctive monitoring indicator for SUD-related psychiatric management. These results offer preliminary correlational evidence for mitigating sleep disruption through anti-inflammatory approaches, warranting further longitudinal and experimental validation.

papers.title: A network-control approach to seizure intervention via adjoint optimal control: a computational study on a connectome-coupled Hopf oscillator model.
papers.abstract: Most existing open-loop Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) systems for drug-resistant epilepsy do not take into account the temporal dynamics of seizures or the spread of seizure activity. In this paper, we propose a closed-loop control system that models seizure prevention as a constraint on the nonlinear dynamics of the brain's structural network, and we evaluate it entirely in simulation. The structural network of the brain is modeled using the HCP-1065 (Human Connectome Project) connectome, which divides the brain into 360 regions. A densely connected sub-network of 60 brain regions was used to develop and test the proposed control system. Each region is modeled as a nonlinear supercritical Hopf oscillator, and the seizures modeled are focal-onset events that spread from a hippocampal onset zone through the connectome. A detector continuously monitors critical-slowing-down features of the dynamics, such as variance and lag-1 autocorrelation, to identify the approach to seizure activity. Two levels of control are applied: a linear-quadratic regulator (Level 1) that maintains the Hopf oscillators' basal state, and a dormant network-wide optimal controller (Level 2) that employs an adjoint-based optimal-control method (Adjoint Optimal Control; AOC) to provide pre-emptive control. Within the model, the predictive detector identifies the approach to the seizure transition with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.889 (95% confidence interval (CI) [0.820, 0.950]) on an independent test fold containing 50 trajectories per class, with a mean lead time of 56.9 model-time seconds; at the recall-maximizing operating point its false-positive rate is high (0.90 per 120-s seizure-free record), which we identify as the principal limitation of the present design. The controller prevented the seizure-like transition in 93% of 100 Monte Carlo simulations (95% CI: 86.2--96.6%) on the 60-node sub-network, against 21% for a connectome-naive targeting baseline; in the same continuously seizure-prone benchmark, a continuous open-loop push at matched amplitude and a PI controller suppressed every trial at lower energy, so the closed loop's advantages lie in pre-emptive lead time, network-wide homeostasis and delivering no stimulation when no risk is detected, not in energy per event. All validation uses synthetic trajectories generated by the same model; no patient or EEG data are used, and the results constitute a methodological proof-of-concept rather than evidence of clinical efficacy.

papers.title: Smartwatch-Derived Biomarkers Signal Pace of Biological Aging.
papers.abstract: Biological aging varies substantially among individuals of the same chronological age, yet biological aging biomarkers require biospecimen collection and laboratory processing, limiting scalability for repeated monitoring. This study evaluated whether consumer smartwatch-derived digital biomarkers are associated with the pace of biological aging, quantified using DunedinPACE, a biomarker that measures biological aging rates. Baseline data were analyzed from the Healthy Minds for Life study within the Precision Aging Network. Among 1305 enrolled participants, 621 community-dwelling adults aged 50-79 years had both DunedinPACE and smartwatch data available. Smartwatch-derived biomarkers were grouped into mobility, cardiorespiratory physiology, sleep, and physiological stress domains. Associations with DunedinPACE were examined using Spearman correlations and adjusted linear regression models. Significant associations were observed across all four domains. Daily step count showed the strongest mobility-domain association with DunedinPACE (r = -0.25, p < 0.01). Mean sleep peripheral oxygen saturation showed the strongest sleep-domain association (r = -0.22, p < 0.01). Resting heart rate showed the strongest physiological stress-domain association (r = 0.24, p < 0.01). Adjusted regression models supported these findings, with lower daily mobility, poorer sleep oxygenation and efficiency, greater wake after sleep onset, and higher resting heart rate showing the most consistent associations with higher DunedinPACE values. Smartwatch-derived biomarkers captured a multidomain profile of accelerated biological aging characterized by lower mobility, poorer sleep health, and elevated physiological stress. Consumer wearables can provide low-burden, real-world indicators of biological vulnerability, although longitudinal studies are needed before clinical use.

papers.title: Adaptation and psychometric properties of the life conditions scale in university staff: a study in Spain and Colombia.
papers.abstract: Health promotion within the university setting requires valid and reliable instruments to identify factors related to lifestyle, emotional well-being and mental health among staff. Although the Life Conditions Scale (LifeConScale) had previously been validated in adolescents, there were no instruments specifically integrating these dimensions for university personnel. Therefore, adaptation and validation for use with higher education professionals is necessary. To adapt the LifeConScale and examine its psychometric properties in university staff, including Teaching and Research Staff and Technical, Management, Administrative and Services Staff. A cross-sectional study was conducted with 440 professionals from two universities in Spain and Colombia. The instrument was adapted via a Delphi process with health and health-promotion experts. Common-factor exploratory factor analysis with parallel analysis and oblique rotation assessed internal structure; Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin and Bartlett's test evaluated sampling adequacy. Reliability was estimated with McDonald's omega. Measurement invariance for core dimensions (personal wellbeing, anxiety, physical activity) between countries was examined through nested multigroup confirmatory factor analysis (configural, metric and scalar). Sampling adequacy was adequate (KMO = 0.850; p < 0.001). Parallel analysis and common-factor exploratory factor analysis with oblique rotation identified seven interpretable factors: personal wellbeing, anxiety, physical activity, snacking, leisure screen use, social media use, and fruit and vegetable intake. The Personal Wellbeing Index and GAD-7 showed no cross-loadings and a moderate latent correlation, supporting discriminant validity; the AUDIT-C was retained as an independent validated scale scored with its original algorithm. Reliability (McDonald's omega) was excellent for anxiety (ω = 0.929), wellbeing (ω = 0.922) and social media (ω = 0.920), and good for physical activity (ω = 0.859), leisure screens (ω = 0.795), fruit and vegetables (ω = 0.760) and snacking (ω = 0.753). Heterogeneous dietary and sleep indicators were treated as formative and not aggregated into summative scores.

papers.title: Between-group differences in resting-state functional connectivity within the brain's extended triple-network following genuine and sham chiropractic adjustments: a quasi-experimental pilot trial.
papers.abstract: Chiropractic research has traditionally focused on subjective, pain-related outcomes; however, emerging evidence suggests that chiropractic care may also influence neurophysiological functioning. This pilot study aimed to assess the feasibility of a neurophysiological assessment battery and explore differences in brain and autonomic nervous system (ANS) responses following genuine versus sham chiropractic adjustments. In this pilot quasi-experimental, sham-controlled trial, 30 adults received a single session of either genuine or sham instrument-assisted chiropractic care. Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) and electrocardiography (ECG) were collected at baseline, immediately post-intervention, and one week later. Feasibility outcomes included study procedures and participant blinding. Exploratory outcomes included changes in EEG functional connectivity (FC) and heart rate variability (HRV). The study protocol was feasible to implement, and participant blinding was successful. Compared with sham care, genuine chiropractic care was associated with increased resting-state FC within a broadly distributed cluster spanning cortical regions of the brain's extended triple-network, including the medial frontoparietal, dorsolateral frontoparietal, and mid-cingulo-insular networks, in the delta and theta frequency bands. No between-group differences were observed for HRV measures. These findings suggest that genuine chiropractic adjustments may differentially influence resting-state functional connectivity within large-scale brain networks compared with sham care. Although no effects on HRV were observed, the neurophysiological findings support further investigation in a fully powered randomized controlled trial to confirm these effects and determine their clinical significance. This trial was prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05249530) and funded by Life University (Marietta, GA, USA).

papers.title: Editorial: Sleep and cognition: the role of sleep patterns and deprivation in memory and learning.
EEG emotion-recognition datasets for neuroarchitecture: an appraisal of openness, AI-readiness and ontology maturity.
papers.abstract: Neuroarchitecture studies how designed space shapes emotion, often with electroencephalography (EEG), and computational models that decode emotion from EEG must be trained on labelled recordings. Yet none of the widely shared EEG emotion datasets was recorded while people moved through designed spaces, and the few spatial recordings we found, all released since 2023, are single studies, each cited at most once. Researchers therefore borrow general emotion datasets, recorded from seated participants watching films, listening to music, playing games or conversing, and must decide whether each can be found, obtained and reused for transfer learning. This review contributes a reusable method for that decision and applies it. Following PRISMA 2020 with the dataset as the unit of analysis, two search passes identified 27 publicly obtainable datasets (22 in the first, 5 in the second), none designed for spatial research. A published codebook of 52 criteria defines three instruments: openness, judged against the FAIR principles with access class recorded separately; AI-readiness, the equally weighted mean of three sub-scores (label information, fit to standard tasks and alignment with other data), which describes usefulness as a transfer source; and ontology maturity, on five levels, which describes how far emotion labels can be mapped onto other vocabularies. Every identifier and access route was checked. Openness was weakest in Interoperability (2.044 against a FAIR composite of 2.857), and only 8 datasets were fully open. A dataset-level identifier was missing for 13 of 27 datasets (48.1%), and three widely used datasets could not be reached through their published routes at a re-check on 11 September 2026. AI-readiness averaged 2.684 on a 1.0-4.0 scale (median 2.60, range 2.10-3.33), and ontology levels concentrated at Level 3 (16 of 27), with none at Level 4 or 5. Openness and readiness were nearly unrelated (ρ = 0.08), whereas ontology level tracked readiness (ρ = 0.68), partly because both read the label structure. Open access alone is therefore a poor guide to reuse. The method, codebook and scripts are published so that researchers in fields without dedicated data can test the datasets they plan to reuse.

papers.title: Study on the association between sleep quality and anxiety-depression symptoms in school-aged children.
papers.abstract: To analyze the short-term longitudinal associations between sleep-related problems and anxiety, depression and the coexistence of anxiety and depression in school-aged children, and to provide the epidemiological evidence for mental health surveillance and risk assessment. This study was part of a child and adolescent growth and development cohort in an urban district of Chongqing. Participants were recruited from grade 1-3 at three local primary schools. A total of 1,529 children (782 boys and 747 girls; average age = 8.00 ± 1.0 years) were included who completed two surveys. Sleep, anxiety, and depressive symptoms were assessed using the PSQI-5, GAD-7, and CDI-S, respectively. Binary logistic regression and multiple linear regression were used to examine the associations between baseline sleep levels, sleep change values (ΔPSQI), and follow-up emotional outcomes. Missing covariates were handled via multiple imputation. The total scores of PSQI-5, GAD-7, and CDI-S at the follow-up were all lower than those at the baseline (p < 0.001). After adjusting for confounding factors and baseline emotional levels, a higher baseline PSQI independently predicted subsequent anxiety (OR = 1.144, p < 0.001), depression (OR = 1.097, p = 0.013), and coexisting symptoms (OR = 1.146, p = 0.003). The increases in ΔPSQI was positively associated with the aggravation of emotional symptoms (all p < 0.001). Long-term poor sleep and decreased sleep quality may increase the risk of internalizing problems in school-aged children.

papers.title: hiPSC-derived new approach methodology (NAM) recapitulates hallmarks of atrial fibrillation.
papers.abstract: Human in vitro models for atrial fibrillation (AF) remain limited in reproducing disease-specific remodeling. We leveraged a human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived atrial cardiomyocyte (hiPSC-aCM) model, which was co-cultured with human atrial cardiac fibroblasts (haCFs) and subjected to an intermittent tachypacing protocol (ITPP) to mimic AF-associated phenotypes. Human iPSC-derived atrial cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-aCMs) were differentiated, purified, matured, and cultured alone or co-cultured with human atrial cardiac fibroblasts at defined seeding ratios (e.g., 90/10 or 70/30 hiPSC-aCM/haCF). Cultures were subjected to 7 days of intermittent tachypacing using electrical field stimulation. Functional electrophysiology and calcium handling were assessed by high-throughput optical mapping, arrhythmia inducibility testing, and genetically encoded or chemical calcium indicators. Structural and molecular remodeling were evaluated by immunocytochemistry, qPCR, and Western blot analysis. ITPP increased spontaneous action potential (AP) frequency and shortened AP duration at 80% repolarization (APD80%), while reducing calcium transient (CaT) upstroke slope and amplitude. Co-cultures at a 70/30 hiPSC-aCM/haCF ratio exhibited marked structural remodeling, with a >100-fold increase in Collagen III expression (P < 0.0001), decreased excitability (ΔHz = -61 ± 6%, P < 0.0001), prolonged APD80% (Δ = +130 ± 10%, P < 0.0001), increased triangulation (ΔAPDTri = +143 ± 13%, P < 0.0001), reduced upstroke slope (Δ = -66 ± 6%, P < 0.0001), conduction block (Δ = -52 ± 18%, P = 0.026), and impaired Ca2⁺ handling (upstroke slope Δ = -50 ± 8%, P < 0.0001; ΔdF/F0 = -34 ± 9%, P = 0.0003). Applying ITPP to the 70/30 co-culture induced AF-like remodeling, with increased spontaneous activity (ΔHz = +25 ± 8%, P = 0.02), shortened APD80% (Δ = -16 ± 6%, P = 0.01), and reduced conduction velocity (ΔCV100/0 vs. 70/30 = -27 ± 15%, P = 0.0005). Mechanistically, ITPP led to downregulation of phospholamban (PLN) and altered PLN-SERCA2a balance, along with upregulation of TGFB1 and natriuretic peptides, reflecting calcium-handling dysfunction and pro-fibrotic signaling. Together, these findings establish a human-relevant platform in 2D culture that recapitulates key AF-associated structural and electrophysiological remodeling for mechanistic studies and therapeutic screening.

papers.title: Effects of an embodied music intervention on executive function, emotion regulation and psychophysiological well-being in children: the role of movement-rhythm synchronization and self-regulation.
papers.abstract: Music participation engages auditory processing, temporal prediction, attention, and motor coordination, but the additional contribution of structured bodily engagement to children's cognitive and emotional development remains unclear. This randomized controlled trial examined whether a 12-week embodied music intervention produced greater changes in executive function, emotion regulation, movement-rhythm synchronization, and psychophysiological well-being than non-embodied music participation or usual activity. A total of 180 children aged 8-11 years were randomly assigned to embodied music (n = 60), non-embodied music (n = 60), or usual-activity control (n = 60). The two music conditions were matched for duration, musical exposure, instructor contact, and session frequency; the embodied condition additionally incorporated whole-body rhythmic coordination, movement inhibition, rule switching, spatial movement, and cooperative synchronization. Assessments were conducted at baseline (T0), week 6 (T1), week 12/post-intervention (T2), and 3-month follow-up (T3). Primary outcomes were executive function and emotion regulation; secondary outcomes included movement-rhythm synchronization, psychological well-being, resting heart rate variability indexed by RMSSD, and sleep problems. Linear mixed-effects models showed significant Group x Time interactions for executive function, chi-square(6) = 78.60, p < 0.001; emotion regulation, chi-square(6) = 51.40, p < 0.001; and movement-rhythm synchronization, chi-square(6) = 129.30, p < 0.001. At T2, embodied music showed larger model-estimated improvements than non-embodied music in executive function [adjusted difference in change = 6.40, 95% CI (3.80, 9.00), p < 0.001], emotion regulation [4.30, 95% CI (2.00, 6.60), p < 0.001], and movement-rhythm synchronization [10.90, 95% CI (8.20, 13.60), p < 0.001]. Benefits were largely maintained at follow-up. Changes in psychological well-being and RMSSD were more moderate, and sleep effects were smaller. Exploratory indirect-effect analyses were statistically consistent with the hypothesized association among embodied music, synchronization, executive function, emotion regulation, and later well-being [standardized serial indirect effect = 0.022, bootstrap 95% CI (0.009, 0.043)]; because the proposed mediators were not fully separated in time, these analyses do not establish temporal or causal mediation. Overall, the randomized comparisons support benefits of embodied music for several proximal outcomes, while the proposed mechanisms require further confirmatory study.

papers.title: Slow power-envelope associations among brain, heart, and gut signals during sleep: an exploratory multivariate transfer entropy study.
papers.abstract: Sleep and the brain-gut axis both involve the coordinated regulation of the central nervous system (CNS), autonomic nervous system (ANS), and enteric nervous system. Although the role of the brain-gut axis in sleep regulation is increasingly recognized, the dynamic information flow and its directionality among the brain, heart, and gut systems during sleep remain unclear as statistical associations. In this study, based on overnight sleep data from 24 healthy subjects, we simultaneously collected occipital electroencephalogram (EEG), electrocardiogram, and bowel sound signals, constructed a multimodal physiological signal analysis framework, and employed a multivariate transfer entropy method based on non-uniform embedding and k-nearest neighbor estimation to systematically quantify directed statistical associations at the level of slow power envelope co-modulations among the brain, heart, and gut systems within the framework of sleep staging. The results reveal a consistent pattern of directed statistical associations: information transfer from heart to brain, brain to gut, and heart to gut consistently exceeds that in the reverse directions across all sleep stages. Sleep-stage dynamics further dissociate within-system from inter-system information flow: internal information exchange within the brain and gut intensifies with sleep depth and weakens during REM, whereas inter-system pathways show divergent stage-dependent patterns: heart-to-brain flow increases from light to deep sleep, while heart-to-gut and brain-to-gut flow are suppressed during deep sleep. At the frequency-band level, the brain, heart, and gut each exhibit dynamically reorganized source-receiver roles across sleep stages, with specific frequency bands contributing differentially to each inter-system pathway depending on sleep stage. This study identifies exploratory statistical patterns of directional information flow among the brain, heart, and gut systems during sleep, providing hypothesis-generating observations for future studies on sleep and multi-organ interactions. These directed associations do not establish anatomical pathways, causal regulation, or clinical biomarkers, and should be regarded as exploratory.

papers.title: An anatomy-guided whole-heart framework for computational modelling of the complete human cardiac conduction system.
papers.abstract: Computational models of cardiac electrophysiology are increasingly used to investigate arrhythmia mechanisms and evaluate therapeutic interventions, yet most existing frameworks omit or oversimplify the cardiac conduction system, limiting their physiological fidelity and clinical applicability. We present a subject-specific, anatomy-guided computational model of the complete human cardiac conduction system (CCS) integrated within a four-chamber heart and torso geometry derived from magnetic resonance imaging. The model comprises a three-dimensional sinoatrial node with discrete exit pathways, interatrial conduction pathways including Bachmann's bundle and posterosuperior connections, an atrioventricular node with explicit fast and slow pathway anatomy, His bundle, left bundle branch with trifascicular configuration, right bundle branch, and fascicle-anchored Purkinje networks. The unknown ramification topology of the Purkinje network was approximated by a partitioned subendocardial surrogate with region-specific isotropic conduction velocities. Whole-heart electrophysiology was simulated using a reaction-eikonal formulation with region-specific ionic models, enabling near real-time computation of cardiac activation and the associated 12-lead electrocardiogram. Simulated activation sequences reproduced physiologically consistent atrial and ventricular depolarisation patterns, including right atrial breakthrough along the crista terminalis, Bachmann's bundle-mediated interatrial conduction, dual-pathway atrioventricular nodal activation, and near-synchronous ventricular depolarisation initiated at the fascicle-myocardial junctions. The simulated 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) demonstrated close qualitative agreement with the measured recording, with particularly strong agreement in QRS morphology and overall correspondence in P-wave morphology. This framework provides an anatomy-guided and computationally tractable platform for investigating conduction system physiology, bundle branch block phenotypes, and conduction system pacing strategies.

papers.title: [Spasticity in Multiple Sclerosis: 2026 Expert Consensus].
papers.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neuroinflammatory disease that significantly impairs quality of life. Spasticity is one of the most frequent and highly disabling features of MS, often accompanied by cramps, pain, bladder dysfunction, sleep disturbances, fatigue, and tremor. Recently, the concept of 'spasticity-plus syndrome' (SPS) has emerged to reflect the interplay among these symptoms. This work aims to update the Spanish clinical guideline for managing MS-related spasticity (MSS) by adopting this evolving concept. A panel of 14 Spanish neurologists assessed the available evidence using a two-level literature review strategy, combining a systematic review focused on SPS with a rapid review of MSS management. Building on the previous guideline, the panel formulated updated recommendations with the scientific endorsement of the Spanish Society of Neurology (SEN). To support a structured and transparent development process, an adapted GRADE-informed framework was used to guide the appraisal of the evidence and formulation of recommendations. A total of nine publications addressing the SPS concept were identified. Based on the evidence and expert consensus, the panel developed 13 recommendations covering triggering and aggravating factors, the diagnosis and evaluation of spasticity, and therapeutic strategies for patient management. In addition, a comprehensive treatment algorithm was proposed to guide therapeutic decision-making according to patients' clinical profiles. This work provides updated recommendations for the management of patients with MSS, integrating the SPS concept into clinical practice. The panel highlights the importance of a symptom-oriented approach that considers the full spectrum of clinical manifestations to individualize treatment, simplify the therapeutic approach, and minimize the risk of polypharmacy.

papers.title: Clinical Outcomes of Nasal Tip Infantile Hemangiomas: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: Infantile hemangiomas (IH) are the most common vascular tumors in infancy. Nasal tip infantile hemangiomas (NTIH) are associated with high-risk disfigurement and long-term sequelae. Despite widespread use of propranolol, optimal management of NTIH remains incompletely defined. A retrospective cohort study included patients with NTIH evaluated between 2003 and 2019 at a pediatric referral center. Inclusion required confirmed diagnosis by two pediatric dermatologists, available clinical photographs, and ≥ 6 months of follow-up. Data collected included demographics, IH subtype, treatments, adverse events, and sequelae at 3 years old. Propranolol-treated patients were stratified by dose (≤ 2.5 vs. > 2.5 mg/kg/day). Fifty-eight patients met inclusion criteria. Propranolol was prescribed in 72.4% (n = 42), with a mean duration of 16.0 months. Adverse effects were predominantly mild (sleep disturbances, 20.7%). At 3 years of age, sequelae, particularly fibroadipose tissue, were significantly less frequent in propranolol-treated patients compared to those untreated (42.9% vs. 91.8%, p = 0.005; overall sequelae: 67.9% vs. 100%, p = 0.037). Sequelae rates did not differ between low- and high-dose propranolol groups. Combined propranolol and topical timolol was associated with increased telangiectatic sequelae, likely reflecting treatment selection bias. No association was found between IH subtype and sequelae. Systemic propranolol was associated with fewer long-term sequelae in NTIH, particularly fibroadipose tissue. A lower dose of 2 mg/kg/day appears sufficient in most cases. Topical timolol may provide limited additional benefit and should not delay propranolol initiation. These findings support early systemic propranolol as the standard of care in NTIH management.

papers.title: Cerebral amyloid PET in obstructive sleep apnoea: a systematic review and exploratory meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate cerebral amyloid-PET findings in adults with obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), account for overlapping cohorts, and quantify global cortical amyloid burden where outcomes were commensurable. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to 17 July 2026 for adult human studies relating OSA or sleep-disordered breathing to cerebral amyloid PET. One estimate per independent data source was retained. The second author independently verified eligibility, cohort independence, extracted quantitative data, and risk-of-bias judgements for all reports entering any quantitative model. Global outcomes were pooled as Hedges' g using restricted maximum-likelihood random-effects models with modified Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals. Fifteen reports representing 12 independent data sources were included. Tracers, reference regions, partial-volume correction, OSA ascertainment, and cognitive status varied substantially. Three global-outcome cohorts of cognitively unimpaired participants (n = 291) yielded g = 0.42 (95% confidence interval, -0.14 to 0.99; I2 = 0%). In a secondary analysis, adding one cohort with established Alzheimer's disease yielded g = 0.54 (95% confidence interval, 0.22-0.86; n = 471; I2 = 0%). A sensitivity model adding one selected regional 11C-PiB estimate yielded g = 0.47 (95% confidence interval, 0.17-0.78). In a secondary analysis combining cognitively unimpaired adults and patients with established Alzheimer's disease, OSA was associated with higher global cerebral amyloid-PET burden. However, the primary evidence in cognitively unimpaired adults remains imprecise, and longitudinal studies do not consistently demonstrate an association between conventional OSA severity and amyloid accumulation.

papers.title: Effects of physical fitness level on cardiac autonomic activity and baroreflex function after maximal lower body negative pressure.
papers.abstract: This study evaluated cardiac autonomic activity and arterial-cardiac baroreflex function before and after severe orthostatic stress induced by lower body negative pressure (LBNP) in healthy sedentary men and endurance athletes. Thirteen healthy sedentary men (Sed) and nine age-matched highly trained male endurance athletes (Fit) were recruited. Participants underwent a single maximal LBNP protocol, with negative pressure increased to -15, -30, and -40 mmHg every 5 min, followed by additional -10 mmHg increments every 3 min until presyncope. RR interval and systolic blood pressure were recorded for 5 min during controlled breathing at 0.2 Hz before and after recovery from maximal LBNP. Heart rate was lower in Fit than in Sed, with no significant pre-to-post change after LBNP. Low-frequency transfer function gain between systolic blood pressure and RR interval showed a significant group-by-time interaction, increasing in Sed (5.9 ± 1.8 to 8.0 ± 1.4 ms/mmHg) but decreasing in Fit (12.2 ± 7.5 to 9.7 ± 5.2 ms/mmHg). Low-frequency RR interval variability also showed a significant interaction, increasing in Sed and decreasing in Fit, whereas high-frequency RR interval variability showed a similar but non-significant pattern. Severe orthostatic stress induced by maximal LBNP enhanced arterial-cardiac baroreflex gain in sedentary men but decreased it in endurance athletes. This response may be associated with enhanced vagally mediated cardiac modulation in sedentary individuals.

papers.title: Sex differences in parietal alpha power during sustained attention are related to conflict monitoring performance in mild cognitive impairment.
papers.abstract: BackgroundSex differences in cognition among individuals with dementias and prodromal stages such as amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI) manifest in variations in severity and prevalence, but underlying brain activity patterns remain unclear. This study is a secondary endpoint study of the Cogmax project.ObjectiveWe examined sex differences in parietal alpha power during an attention task (Simple Vigilance Task, SVT) and its association with conflict monitoring (Stroop Color-Word Test Part 3, T score) in individuals with aMCI.MethodsThe SVT served as the EEG recording condition because of its low cognitive demands and visually driven structure, while the Stroop task provided an independent neuropsychological measure of conflict monitoring. Seventy-seven participants (23 females; 54 males) were included. We analyzed average power spectral density (PSD) across occipital and parietal electrodes (O1-Pz-O2-P7-P8) using multitaper Fourier transform. Normalized alpha power was calculated as integrated 7-11 Hz relative to total 0.1-40 Hz PSD.ResultsAll participants showed high accuracy on the SVT, indicating stable attentional engagement. Covariate-adjusted permutation tests, robust to unbalanced sample sizes, showed that females exhibited higher parietal alpha power and higher Stroop Part 3 T-scores than males. However, when Stroop performance was included as a covariate, the sex difference in alpha power became nonsignificant. A positive correlation between Stroop 3 scores and parietal alpha power was observed in females but not in males, suggesting a sex-specific relationship.ConclusionsParietal alpha activity may be associated with conflict monitoring performance in aMCI, particularly among females, providing evidence for sex-related neural differences in aMCI.

papers.title: Cardiometabolic, Physiological and Objective-Sleep Responses to Transcendental Meditation: Secondary Analysis of a Randomised Controlled Trial Among University Staff.
papers.abstract: Chronic stress contributes to cardiometabolic risk, and stress-reduction interventions have been proposed to improve stress-sensitive physiology and cardiometabolic health, though evidence remains inconsistent. This study examined the effects of a Transcendental Meditation (TM) intervention on cardiometabolic health and upstream physiological outcomes. This two-arm, open-label RCT compared TM (n = 65) with control (access to university well-being resource, n = 64) among Australian university staff. Secondary outcomes included blood pressure (BP), fasting glucose, HOMA insulin resistance (IR), lipids, C-reactive protein, salivary cortisol, heart rate variability (HRV), sympathetic arousal, and a post hoc composite cardiometabolic risk (CMR) score. Post hoc exploratory analyses tested whether burnout, sex and baseline metabolic risk moderated TM effects on HRV, total cholesterol, cortisol slope and IR. Primary analyses were intention-to-treat. TM was associated with a small diastolic BP reduction (-1.18 mmHg [95% CI: -2.35, -0.01], interaction p = 0.036), with a non-significant trend in the endpoint-only analysis (p = 0.064); no other outcomes differed between groups. Burnout moderated the HRV response (p = 0.02), favouring higher-burnout participants and sex moderated the cholesterol response (p = 0.011), with TM attenuating the control-group rise in females, with uncertainty on LDL and HDL. Interactions for cortisol slope (by sex) and HOMA-IR (by metabolic risk) were non-significant; stratified comparisons suggested numerically greater improvement in TM males and higher-risk participants, respectively. Given no multiplicity correction, all findings are hypothesis-generating only. TM was associated with small, non-robust diastolic BP reduction with no effect on other outcomes. Burnout may modify HRV response, but this finding requires confirmation in adequately powered trials. ACTRN12625000134426.

papers.title: Compassion Fatigue and Perceived Organizational Performance: Emergency Nurses' Wellbeing as a Mediating Factor.
papers.abstract: Compassion fatigue is a widespread professional issue in nursing practice, yet the wider organizational implications of compassion fatigue, especially its association with perceived organizational performance through nurses' wellbeing, are not fully investigated in the context of Egyptian critical care. Clarifying this pathway is important for designing targeted managerial interventions that can maintain the wellbeing of the staff and the efficiency of the institution. To investigate the mediating effect of nurses' wellbeing on the relationship between compassion fatigue and perceived organizational performance among critical care and emergency nurses. A descriptive correlational cross-sectional study was undertaken with 111 nurses who worked in intensive care (54.1%), emergency (13.5%), and other inpatient and outpatient units of Alexandria Main University Hospital, Egypt. Three validated data collection instruments were used to collect data between July and September 2024, namely, the Professional Quality of Life (ProQOL) Secondary Traumatic Stress (STS) subscale, used to measure compassion fatigue (10 items, 5-point Likert scale; α = 0.868); the Organizational Performance Questionnaire, which captures perceived organizational performance (11 items, 5-point Likert scale; α = 0.944); and the Nurse Wellbeing Scale (17 items, 10-point Likert-type scale; α = 0.945). The tools were subject to intensive translation, content validation, exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis (AMOS 23.0), and reliability testing. Associations were examined with Pearson correlation and regression-based mediation analysis (PROCESS Model 4; 5000 bootstrap samples). Most nurses (65.8%) expressed a low degree of compassion fatigue (mean = 2.70 ± 0.74), and 44.1% perceived organizational performance as low (mean = 3.04 ± 0.84). Nurses' wellbeing was low (mean = 4.02 ± 1.98 on the 1-10 scale), with the largest gaps in physical self-care interventions, such as exercise, sleep, or mindfulness, and lack of manager-nurse communication about wellbeing. Compassion fatigue had a significant negative correlation with perceived organizational performance (r = -0.400, p < 0.001) and wellbeing (r = -0.513, p < 0.001). In the mediation analysis, higher compassion fatigue was significantly associated with lower wellbeing (B = -2.329, p < 0.001), and that wellbeing was a positive predictor of perceived organizational performance (B = 0.154, p < 0.001). After accounting for wellbeing, the direct effect of compassion fatigue on perceived organizational performance was nonsignificant (B = -0.140, 95% CI [-0.356, 0.077], p = 0.196), whereas the indirect effect through wellbeing was significant (B = -0.360, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.545, -0.227]), indicating that wellbeing statistically mediated 72.0% of the total effect. Nurses' wellbeing statistically mediated the association between compassion fatigue and perceived organizational performance. Because of the cross-sectional design, these findings indicate associations rather than causal effects, and longitudinal studies are needed to confirm the pathway. Systematic, frequent screening for compassion fatigue using instruments such as the ProQOL is recommended, together with organizational-level interventions that address self-care deficits such as protected scheduling and resources dedicated to wellbeing. Supporting leadership, creating psychologically safe workplaces, implementing formal peer support networks, and infusing compassion fatigue prevention into education are recommended to support nurse wellbeing and perceived organizational performance, although these recommendations require testing in longitudinal and interventional studies.

papers.title: Sex-based differences in the atrial fibrillation care pathway and outcomes: an ITHACA-database analysis.
papers.abstract: To characterize sex-specific differences in clinical presentation, evaluate progression through the atrial fibrillation (AF) care pathway from diagnosis to catheter ablation (CA) and assess long-term outcomes. This was a retrospective cohort study of patients with incident AF at Northwell Health between 2015 and 2024 from the ITHACA-database. Sex-specific differences in clinical presentation were examined. The AF care pathway was operationalized as a stepwise cascade, modelling conditional drop-off to identify care gaps. Sex-specific CA risk ratios were assessed via Poisson regression. Incident AF was identified among 165 563/655 459 patients (71.4 ± 11.6 years, 32% non-white, 45% female) with a recorded diagnosis of AF. Women were older (73.3 ± 10.6 vs. 69.8 ± 12.1 years, P < 0.001), had higher rates of dementia (9.1% vs. 5.2%), stroke (8.6% vs. 7.4%) and congestive heart failure (21.5% vs. 20.8%) at diagnosis. Transfer-of-care gaps [median 3.6 years follow-up, 96% retention] were identified at every level: 31.5% of women vs. 35.3% of men were evaluated by cardiology, 16.2% vs. 21.6% by electrophysiology, and 3.5% vs. 5.7% underwent CA (all P < 0.001). Women were 16% less likely to receive CA (RR 0.84 95% CI 0.77-0.91). In cause-specific Cox models, female sex was associated with incident stroke (aHR 1.24, 95% CI 1.18-1.30) and dementia (aHR 1.30, 95% CI 1.24-1.35), but modestly lower mortality after adjustment (aHR 0.96, 95% CI 0.94-0.99). In this real-world analysis, significant sex-specific differences in clinical phenotype at presentation, progression through the AF care pathway and clinical outcomes were observed.
